newsitem.title: USA: Clinton budget proposes $98 billion in tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton budget proposes $98 billion in tax cuts.

text.p: President Clinton this week will unveil a budget combining $98 billion in tax cuts with $80 billion in tax rises and aiming to balance by 2002 -- provided he can cut a deal with the Republican-led Congress.

U.S. officials on Sunday began the process of selling the fiscal 1998 budget, which covers the year beginning on Oct. 1 and which is not scheduled to be made public until Thursday, when Clinton sends it to Congress.
Franklin Raines, director of the Office of Management and Budget, said on Sunday the budget would include $98 billion in tax cuts designed to encourage education and home ownership.
"It's going to be a very targeted tax cut programme that I think is going to make a meaningful difference for American families," Raines told NBC's "Meet the Press" programme.

Confirming what other officials have said privately, Raines said the proposals would include offering a $1,500 tax credit for college tuition and extending the capital gains tax exclusion on home sales to $500,000 per couple.

Administration officials last week told Reuters the tax cuts would be partly offset by about $80 billion in higher revenues, including restoring an expired airport excise tax and closing a variety of corporate tax loopholes.
Despite the fact that the budget will therefore have a net tax cut of roughly $20 billion, officials on Sunday said they were intent on balancing the budget by the year 2002.

"Our first priority is to finish the job to balance the budget," White House chief of staff Erskine Bowles told the National Governors Association. "These deficits that we have run in this country have robbed the economy of billions."
But to do so Clinton, a Democrat, will have to win the backing of Congress, both of whose houses are controlled by the Republicans.
Raines said he was "quite optimistic" it would be possible to balance the budget, a sentiment cautiously echoed by several prominent Republicans despite the differences between the two parties.

"I am very hopeful," said Sen. Pete Domenici, the New Mexico Republican who chairs the Senate budget committee. "I will do everything I can to see if we can do it, but I don't want anybody to think we're going to get a balanced budget and agree with the president if some of our basic philosophies have to be modified and thrown out -- thrown down the river."

"I praise the president for the direction he is heading. But I remain concerned that the tax cuts are temporary while the tax hikes are permanent," said Republican Bill Archer of Texas, who chairs the powerful House Ways and Means Committee. "As a result the total tax package may add up to another tax increase -- not tax relief. Important questions remain."

Simply stated, the Republicans want a larger and broader tax cut than Clinton advocates, as well as a more dramatic effort to rein in entitlements like the Medicare and Medicaid health care programmes for the elderly and the poor.

Independent budget analysts have said Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget appears to hew closely to last year's fiscal 1997 proposal, describing this as a cautious negotiating strategy before the start of real negotiations with the Republicans.

"It is a particularly good opening position if you think that the submission of your budget isn't the end game, but is just the tactical thing to do pending the opening of serious budget negotiations," said Burson-Marsteller's Stan Collender.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, the Republican from Mississippi who will be one of Clinton's key interlocutors on the budget, told ABC's "This Week" programme he soon plans to invite Clinton to come to Capitol Hill to begin negotiations.

"This is (to) sort of sit down and say, Mr. President, it's time that we stopped the little pigeon steps around here, and let's begin to see what we can really do to move some things forward for the American people," Lott said.
